title: Code of Hammurabi: Prologue (obverse, columns i-v)
source: Louvre Sb 8 photographs (Wikimedia Commons; CDLI montage) + CDLI P249253 transliteration + R. F. Harper's 1904 English
description: The prologue of the Code of Hammurabi (c. 1754 BCE), in which Hammurabi names the gods who called him to rule and the cities he cared for, shown column by column on the Louvre stele.
introduction:
The Code of Hammurabi is the longest and best preserved law collection of ancient Mesopotamia. Hammurabi, king of Babylon (c. 1792-1750 BCE), had it carved on basalt stelae late in his reign. The stele in the Louvre (Sb 8) is 2.25 m high. At the top Hammurabi stands before the seated sun god Shamash, god of justice; below, the text runs in horizontal bands, called columns, read from right to left with the signs set upright in the old monumental manner. The stele was carried off to Susa in Elam as war booty in the 12th century BCE and found there by the French mission of Jacques de Morgan in 1901-1902. Many of its laws touch matters also treated in the law of Moses in the Old Testament, such as false witness, theft, kidnapping, slaves, deposits, goring oxen and the rule of like for like (Exodus 21-23, Leviticus 24, Deuteronomy 19-25).

The prologue fills obverse columns i to v line 25. It tells how the gods Anu and Enlil (Bel) gave Marduk rule over mankind and called Hammurabi 'to cause justice to prevail in the land, to destroy the wicked and the evil, to prevent the strong from oppressing the weak', and then lists the cities and temples of his kingdom that he restored and provided for, from Nippur and Eridu to Ashur and Nineveh.

Each section below gives the Akkadian lines of the stele as transliterated by CDLI, with column and line numbers, R. F. Harper's English of 1904, and the photograph of the column that carries those lines. On the obverse each column is shown twice: a colour crop of the band on the stone (the column is the band in the middle of the image) and the same column in the photographic montage of the whole inscription distributed by CDLI, where every column is turned upright and labelled at the top. Reverse columns are shown in the montage. A law that runs over from one column into the next lists both.
translator_notes: Akkadian: CDLI transliteration of the Louvre stele. Square brackets mark signs lost on the stone; # marks a damaged sign and ! a sign the editors correct, as in the source.
Line labels such as 'v 26' give the stele column and line. The obverse has 16 legible columns and the reverse 28; seven further obverse columns were erased in antiquity.
English: R. F. Harper (1904), from the Wikisource transcription corrected against the printed book where the two differ. Harper's words in parentheses are his own additions for sense.
Harper numbers the reverse columns continuously after the 16 obverse columns, so his col. 41 is reverse column xxv.
Harper divides laws 133 and 176 into 133 and 133A, 176 and 176A; CDLI keeps one law number for each, so both parts appear in one section. Laws 242 and 243 form one law in both.

translation.text: When the lofty Anu, king of the Anunnaki, and Bel, lord of heaven and earth, he who determines the destiny of the land, committed the rule of all mankind to Marduk, the chief son of Ea; when they made him great among the Igigi; when they pronounced the lofty name of Babylon; when they made it famous among the quarters of the world and in its midst established an everlasting kingdom whose foundations were firm as heaven and earth—at that time, Anu and Bel called me, Hammurabi, the exalted prince, the worshiper of the gods, to cause justice to prevail in the land, to destroy the wicked and the evil, to prevent the strong from oppressing the weak, to go forth like the Sun over the Black Head Race, to enlighten the land and to further the welfare of the people. Hammurabi, the governor named by Bel, am I, who brought about plenty and abundance; who made everything for Nippur and Durilu complete; the exalted supporter of E-kur; the wise king, who restored Eridu to its place; who purified

The English is cut at Harper's own column markers '(Col. II)' etc., which he placed where the column begins in his rendering; English word order does not follow the Akkadian line by line.

translation.text: (Col. III); who extended the limits of Cutha; who enlarged Shid-lam in every way; the mighty bull, who gores the enemy; the beloved of Tu-tu; who made the city of Borsippa beautiful; the exalted one who was untiring for the welfare of Ezida; the divine city king, wise and intelligent, who extended the settlements of Dilbat; who stored up grain for the mighty Urash; the lord adorned with scepter and crown, whom the wise god Ma-ma has clothed with complete power; who defined the confines of Kish; who made sumptuous the splendid banquets in honor of Nin-tu; the wise and perfect one, who determined the pasture and watering places for Shir-pur-la (Lagash) and Girsu; who provided large sacrifices for the Temple of Fifty; who seizes the enemy; the favorite of the exalted god (oracle); who put into execution the laws of Aleppo; who makes joyful the heart of Anunit; the illustrious prince, the lifting up of whose hands Adad recognizes; who pacifies the heart of Adad, the warrior, in Karkar; who re-established the appointments in E-ud-gal-gal; the king who gave life to Ud-nun-ki; the benefactor of the temple E-mah; the lordly city king; the soldier who has no equal;

translation.text: (Col. IV) who presented life to the city of Mashkan-shabri; who poured out abundance over Shid-lam; the wise governor, who captured the bandit caves (?), who provided a hiding-place for the people of Malka in their misfortune; who founded dwelling-places for them in plenty; who determined for all time the splendid sacrifices for Ea and Dam-gal-nunna, who had extended his dominion; the city king first in rank; who subdued the settlements along the Euphrates; the warrior of Dagan, his creator; who protected the people of Mera and Tutul; the exalted prince, who makes the face of Nana to shine; who established splendid banquets for Nin-a-zu; who helps his people in time of need; who establishes in security their property in Babylon; the governor of the people, the servant, whose deeds are pleasing to Anunit; who installed Anunit in E-ul-mash in Agane broadway; who made justice prevail and who ruled the race with right; who returned to Ashur its gracious protecting deity; who made the rising sun (?) to shine brilliantly; the king who made the name of Nana glorious in E-mish-mish in Nineveh: the exalted one, who makes supplication to the great gods; the descendant of Sumulailu, the powerful son of Sinmu-ballit

translation.text: (Col. V), the ancient seed of royalty, the powerful king, the Sun of Babylon, who caused light to go forth over the lands of Sumer and Akkad; the king, who caused the four quarters of the world to render obedience; the favorite of Nana, am I. When Marduk sent me to rule the people and to bring help to the country, I established law and justice in the land and promoted the welfare of the people.
